title: Brilliant Genius!
summary: Underpromote with check so the knight can fork the rook and then protect the remaining pawn.

nodes.question: Which promotion preserves Black’s win?
nodes.explanation: The bishop has been sacrificed and captured on e4. Black’s b2 pawn is ready to promote, but a queen can be skewered against Kc1.

branches.title: Promote with check and fork from c3
commentary: Begin after Rxe4 in the six-piece final phase. The earlier larger position and bishop sacrifice remain source context.
b1=N+ underpromotes with check against Ka3. The tempo forces White to move its king before saving the rook.
Ka4 is the illustrated king escape. The black king on c1 prevents an escape to b2.
Nc3+ forks Ka4 and Re4, using the knight’s second checking tempo.
Ka5 is an independently selected legal escape from the checking fork.
Nxe4 removes the rook and protects c5. Black has an exactly checked winning knight-and-pawn ending despite the initially smaller promotion choice.

branches.title: The king escapes toward b3
commentary: Compare the source’s other illustrated fork square after promotion. The final king retreat and rook capture are independently completed here.
b1=N+ checks Ka3 immediately, denying White a free rook move.
Kb3 changes the fork square that Black needs.
Nd2+ checks Kb3 and attacks Re4. The fork works from d2 rather than c3.
Ka3 is an independently selected legal retreat from the check.
Nxe4 collects the rook and guards c5. This exact ending is winning for Black.

branches.title: Promote to a queen instead
commentary: Compare the source’s warning about a queen promotion; its skewer is independently completed with a representative king retreat.
b1=Q gives away Black’s win. It does not check Ka3, leaving White time for a rook skewer.
Re1+ checks Kc1 along the first rank with Qb1 behind it.
Kd2 is an independently selected legal king response. The queen remains exposed on b1.
Rxb1 removes the queen. This exact rook-and-pawn ending is winning for White, so maximum promotion material actually reverses the result.

exercises.prompt: Why does a knight outperform a queen here?
exercises.answer: b1=N gives check and forces the king onto a square that permits a second checking fork of Re4. A queen gives no check and allows Re1+ to skewer it behind Kc1.

exercises.prompt: Why does Nxe4 help beyond winning the rook?
exercises.answer: From e4 the knight also protects c5. Black can bring its king forward without immediately losing that remaining pawn.
